SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, the first poin t is that the figure which he is 
referring to pertains to the Ninth Five-Year Plan. In the tenth Five-Year Plan, 
the total focus of the scheme has been changed and now we are developing 
hubs of culture, tourism and good civic life. In the Ninth Five-Year Plan the total 
number of projects sanctioned for Rajasthan were 72 out of which 53 are still 
incomplete and the total cost which has been indicated by me is Rs. 11.64 
crores. But the hon. Member wants to know whether Rajasthan has been fairly 
treated or not. In fact, out of these plans which I have with me, I have given at 
least one great hub of culture, touris m and good civic life in every State. In 
Rajasthan I have given three—Kumbhalgarh, Chittorgarh and Jaisalmer—and a 
separate triangle around Shikhavati Bikaner temple is being worked out. Now, 
there is a total investment of Rs. 18 cr ores during the last eight months and I 
have given the figures which include Dilwada with Rs. 3 crores, Chitrakoot, Rs.

that, investments have been made at Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh. And these 
projects are being directly handled by us . In the Ninth Five-Year Plan, the total

the maximum investment has been made fo r Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and 
Gujarat.

Higher interest rates in RRBs 
*382. SHRI RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that interest rates in Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) 
are higher than those of commercial banks; and 
(b) if so, the action proposed to take up the right type of restructuring plan 
for RRBs? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) A Statem ent is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) The interest rate structure of  Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) is 
generally more or less similar to that of the commercial banks/sponsor 
banks operating in their area of operation. 
As part of financial sector reforms, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
deregulated the interest rate structure in the Banking Sector. The Board of 
Directors of each RRB is free to decide t heir interest rate structure taking into 
account the cost of funds, competitive rates in their command area, yield of 
loans/investments, establishment cost, etc. 
(b) To facilitate strengthening and revitalisation of RRBs the following 
policy initiatives have been taken:— 
• recapitalisation of 187 RRBs; 
• diversification of business portfolio and activities; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
• rationalisation of branch network including relocation and merger 
of loss-making branches; and 
• providing greater role to the sponsor banks in the management 
of RRBs. 
Further, Government had constituted a Working Group to review the 
RRB Act, 1976. The Working Group was required to review the progress in 
dispensation of rural credit especialy through RRBs since their inception and 
to make detailed recommendations in regard to legal, regulatory, supervisory, 
institutional and technological dimensions for making RRBs-an effective 
instrument for development and growth of the rural economy. The Working 
Group has submitted its report to Government, which is under consideration. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, I would like to know whether some 
of the RRBs have closed shop and shifted to towns, without redeploying the 
resources in the rural areas where they we re mobilised, as is evident from the 
low credit-deposit ratio of 41 % and the in vestment-deposit ratio of 70%. What 
type of reforms are proposed in respect of the Regional Rural Banks in order 
to benefit the weaker sections of the society? 
SHRi JASWANT SINGH: Sir, as for the figures the hon. Member has 
cited, about certain specif ic RRBs, it is altogether different. But, so far as 
reform or reforming the Regional Rural Banks is concerned, the hon. Member 
knows that the Chalapati Rao Committee, which was constituted to go into this 
question, has given its recommendations. Without taking much time of the 
House, I can share with the h on. Members some of the major 
recommendations of the Committee. Ther e is recommendation for change in 
the capital structure and ownership pattern , about the structural consolidation, 
about the size of the Board and the role  and functions of the Chairman and 
also regulatory framework and capital adequacy. It is a very comprehensive 
Report. There has been some improvement in the last decade or so in the 
functioning of the RRBs, and we will continue to monitor the progress of the 
RRBs. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir,  my second supplementary is, 
whether the merger of weak RRBs with commercial banks has proved 
beneficial. If so, the details thereof. In case of merger, how will the promotion 
problems of the staff of RRBs would be solved? 
8 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Si r, compared to the commercial banks, the 
origin of the RRBs is different. The RRBs were really started—or meant 
specifically—for lending to the farming community, artisans, etc. Then, around 
1993-94, they were brought into the pattern of large commercial banking 
sector; and now they really operate as any ordinary bank. But, so far as the total 
percentage to agriculture lending is concerned, the RRBs are contributing only 
about seven per cent to the agricultural sector, 41 or 43 per cent is being provided 
by the cooperative banks; and 52 per cent is being provided by the commercial 
banks. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, the hon. Minister has stated in the last 
part of his answer that one of the terms and conditions of the Working Group)—
this Group was setup to review the RRB Act of 1976, and its Report is how

rural credit, the RRBs were established on 2nd October, 1975. May I know from

available with the hon. Minister—What percentage of rural credit is today 
institutionalised through the RRBs and through other institutional arrangements,

what percentage of rural credit is given through the institutional mechanism. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, just now, I gave the percentage. Of course, 
the hon. Member is quite right, as he had been the country's Finance Minister, 
that lt the establishment of Regional Rural Banks was, without doubt, motivated 
by the factor of providing a specific instrument for agricultural lending, for rural 
lending. Thereafter, in 1993-94 or so, when whole nature of RRBs was 
changed, and as of now—I shared it with the hon. Members—the percentage of 
rural agricultural credit which is being provided by the RRBs is only about seven 
per cent of the total; 52 per cent is being provided by the commercial banks; 
and about 41 per cent is being provided by the cooperative banks. The 
Chalapati Rao Committee's recommendations have been received, and I have 
no difficulty in sending you a copy of the recommendations.

Permission for opening Foreign Currency (Domestic) Account 
*394. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE A ND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Governm ent with a view to further liberalise 
foreign exchange facilities have decided to permit resident Indians to open, 
hold and maintain foreign currency (domestic) account with any Nationalised 
Bank; 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
(c) whether any limit has been fixed for retaining money in the proposed 
foreign currency (domestic) account in US Dollars; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
36 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) Yes Sir. As a significant step towards further 
liberalization of foreign exchange facilities available to individual residents, the 
RBI has permitted a person resident in India, to open, hold and maintain with 
an Authorized Dealer in India a Foreign Currency Account known as Resident 
Foreign Currency (Domestic) Account. Foreign Exchange acquired from any of 
the following sources can be kept in this account by Residents: 
(i) while on visit to any place outside India by way of payment for 
services not arising from any business in-or anything done in India; 
or 
(ii) from any person not resident in Indi a and who is on a visit to India, as 
honorarium or gift or for services rendered or in settlement of any 
lawful obligation; or 
(iii) by way of honorarium or gift while on a visit to any place outside India; 
or 
(iv) represents the unspent amount of foreign exchange acquired by him 
from an authorized person for travel abroad. 
This new facility is in addition to the existing facility of retaining US$2000 
or its equivalent in the form of currency notes and/or foreign currency travellers 
cheques. The balance in Resident Foreign currency (Domestic) account may 
be used for any purpose permissible under the current foreign exchange 
regulations for resident Indians (e.g. travel, medical treatment abroad, gifts upto 
US$ 5000, purchase of books directly or through the internet, education abroad, 
etc.) 
There is no limit on balances kept in Resident Foreign Currency 
(Domestic) Account. This account will be maintained in the form of a current 
account only with cheque facility.

Financial crisis in Maharashtra 
2749. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item, 
"Crisis downgrades Maharashtra to default category", which appeared in the 
'Indian Express' dated the 17th October, 2002; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) what steps are proposed to be taken to address the various 
problems and bottlenecks ment ioned in the news article to rectify the financial 
crisis in Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) The article in 
the Indian Express dated 17th October, 2002 referes to the downgraded credit 
rating of the bonds issued by the Public Sector Undertakings under 
Government of Maharashtra in view of their inability to meet in time the payment 
of interest and principal obligations, due to sagging financial condition of the 
State Government. 
(b) and (c) The financial crisis faced by some States including 
Government of Maharashtra has received the attention of Government of India. 
Though the primary responsibility for the repayment of debt of State 
Government rests with respective States and the State Governments are 
expected to take adequate measures to improve their financial conditions, 
Government of India has been facilitating the States to overcome their temporary 
cash imbalance problems by making feasible releases of the State's entitlements 
in advance. 
Besides to enable fiscal consolidation, the Government of India have 
enjoined States to draw up Medium Term Fiscal Reforms Programmes 
(MTFRP) which is projected to bring down the consolidated debt of States. The 
build-up of debt and issuance of guarantees in future has been strictly capped by 
the MTFRPs, and require specific permission of Government of India u nder 
Article 293(3) of the Constitution. 
Government of Maharashtra has drawn up their Medium Term Fiscal Reform 
Programme. Further, the Government of India has since put 
102 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
forward a proposal for debt swap to enable the States to retire high cost debt so 
as to supplement their efforts towards fiscal consolidation.

2752. SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Wi ll the Minister of FINANCE AND

COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) to (c) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that the lending rates of banks have

Risk-Based Supervision for Banks 
2759. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Reserve Bank of India propose to introduce Risk Based 
Supervision (RBS) for banks and to put in place a Prompt Corrective Action 
(PCA) mechanism; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the fresh steps taken for developm ent of a risk profile and designing 
a customary supervisory action plan for each bank? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Risk Based Supervison (RBS) for commercial banks will enhance and 
refine supervisory practices and bring them in line with international best 
practices. The objective of RBS is to ensure stablity of the banking 
123 

RAJYA  SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
system, to promote efficiency, protect the interests of the depositors and prevent 
the misuse of banking system RBS will help Banks in identifying deficiencies in 
systems and controls and to find out appropriate solutions. 
Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) is mechanism based on a pre-
determined rule-based structured early intevention machanism. PCA is 
intended to enhance the effectiveness of the existing supervisory frame-work. It 
has a schedule of corrective action based on three important parameters i.e. 
CRAR, net Non-Performing Assets and Return on Assets, representing capital 
adequacy, asset quality and profitability respectively. Certain trigger points have 
been determined under these parameters and for every trigger point, a set of 
structured and discretionary actions has been proposed, which are designed to 
pre-empt any deterioration in the soundness of banks. 
(c) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has developed a detailed risk profile 
template for compilation of risk profiles of commercial banks under RBS. The 
commercial banks have also been advised by RBI to undertake a self-
assessment of their own risk profiles . A tailor-made supervisory programme 
will be prepared for each bank based on its risk profile.

Royalty on crude Oil 
2779. DR. A.K. PATEL: Will t he Minister of PETROLEUM and 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Question 
3007 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 18th December, 2001 and state: 
(a) what is the rate of royalty on crude oil and gas in the NELP; 
(b) whether these rates are less than the prevailing royalty rates; 
(c) if so, whether there is any move by the Central Government to 
compensate; and 
(d) what is the lower royalty rates payable to the State Government? 
142 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) As per the provisions of 
the Oilfields (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 and Petroleum and 
Natural Gas Rules, 1959 the royalty on crude oil shall not exceed 20% of the sale 
price at well head and 10% of the value at well head of natural gas obtained by 
lessee. Royalty from offshore areas is paid to the Central Government and from 
onland areas to the concerned State Government. 
Under the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP), royalty rate for 
offshore areas is 10% for both crude oil and natural gas. In case of deep water 
areas (beyond 400 metre isobath), the rate of royalty is 5% for crude oil and 
natural gas for the first seven years from the date of commencement of 
commercial production in the field. For onland area, royalty rate is 12.5% for 
crude oil and 10% for natural gas. 
(b) and (d) The royalty rate for natural gas for onland areas is the same 
i.e. 10% under NELP as well as for the gas producing areas in main of Oil and 
Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd. (OIL), allotted to them on 
nomination basis. Royalty on crude oil prevailing at present is specific @Rs.850 
per metric tonne on adhoc basis w.e.f. 01.12.99. 
(c) The onland blocks under NELP have been offered after obtaining 
concurrence of the concerned State Gove rnment to the fiscal terms of NELP, 
including royalty rates for oil and gas.

Loss due to delay in completion of SSP 
2817. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the delay in Sardar Sarovar Project has 
already cost the nation over Rs. 9,125 crore due to operational cost and 
associated expenses as reported in the 'Assam Tribune' dated the 16th 
September, 2002; 
(b) whether the project was scheduled to be completed by January, 1998 
and it is incurring an average loss of Rs. 5 crore a day since then; and 
(c) the shares of Madhya Pr adesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and 
Rajasthan in the benefits of the multipurpose project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
construction of the Sardar Sarovar Dam could not be completed by January, 
1998 as originally planned due to the Writ Petition filed by the Narmada 
Bachao Andolan in the year 1994, the judgement on which was given in 
October, 2000 only. The original estimated cost of the Project as 1986-87 price-
level was Rs. 6406.04 crore, which at 1991-92 price level was Rs. 13,180 crore. 
The estimated cost of the Project at current price-level which is under 
finalisation by the Government of Gujarat is likely to go beyond Rs. 20,000 
crore. Except for a small quantum of water being drawn from the partially 
completed irrigation bye-pass tunnel, no part of the Sardar Sarovar Project can 
be considered as put into operation t ill date. Hence, the question of operational 
cost and associated expenses on the project does not arise. Nevertheless, it 
may be stated that the delay in cons truction of the project has caused the 
nation significant loss on account of project cost escalation, apart from the loss of 
accruable benefits for the period of delay in commissioning different 
components of the project. Thus, the accruable benefits from completed project 
may be considered as likely losses on account of overall delay in construction 
and as per the information made available by the Government of Gujarat such 
annual losses in agricultural production, electricity generation and water supply 
work out to about Rs. 2175 crore, which is equal to a loss of about Rs. 6 crore 
per day.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving 
me this opportunity to share some of my perceptions in regard to these two 
Bills, the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2001 and the Companies (Second 
Amendment) Bill, 2001. While making his observations, one of my colleagues 
has suggested that there should be a comprehensive company legislation for 
corporate governance. In fact, in the last three or four years, we have 
attempted to do exactly that. One of  the major amendments, which was 
related to the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1997, was done in 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
two stages. Mr. Jaitley was then the Minister - in - charge and I had the 
privilege of presiding ov er the Standing Committee which considered the two 
BilIs. One was, of course, relating to ta king out certain sections to facilitate 
buy-back arrangements and investments in the parent company shares. And 
the other amendment was really very comprehensive. If somebody goes back 
to the history of the Company Laws, he will find that it has almost taken 40 
years to make the major amendments. Fi rst in 1916, thereafter in 1956 and, 
thereafter, initiatives were taken in 1977 and when the legislative process is 
completed through these two Bills, I think this exercise will be over. 
In this connection, I would like to point out that while undertaking the 
major amendments in the Company Law, the question of insolvency and 
winding up, expeditious methods of winding up, also arose. But, at that point of 
time, since the recommendations of the Eradi Committee were not available to 
the Government or to the Standing Comm ittee, it was decided to take it up 
later on. And, in fact, the Government  brought out this piece of amendment 
after the recommendations of the Eradi Committee were available. 
One of the major reasons, which we shall have to keep in view, is 
that why the process of winding up shou ld be expedited. Apart from any other 
things, harassment of the individuals concerned, there are two major aspects 
which sometimes fail to get due attention. First is that the productive assets 
get unlocked and remain unlocked for a very long period of time, if the 
dissolution does not take place expeditiously. Secondly, most of the time, it 
has been found that the assets are frittered away and completely wasted and, 
Sir, if you look at the figures, which are indicated in the report itself, you will be 
astonished to find out that in number of  cases, it has taken 15 years, 20 years 
or 25 years. Now what assets would re main intact for a period of 20 or 25 
years? 
Sir, upto 31st December, 1999, the age-wise classification under 
winding up process has been given. Fo r the o to 5 years, there are 1065 
cases, for 5 to 10 years, there are 603 cases, for 10 to 15 years, there are 482 
cases, for 15-20 years, there are 321 cases, for 20-25 years, there are 251 
cases and for 25 years and above, the figure is 473 cases. The simple point is 
after all that the country has invested a lot in creating certain assets, the 
productive potentiality of which is not being utilised and they just get simply 
wasted. 
254 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Therefore, it was considered nece ssary that expeditious measures 
should be taken. We have discussed on a number of occasions about pending 
cases in the High Court. Special attention cannot be paid by the High Courts to 
dispose of the cases in the winding proc ess despite whatever we may like to 
have, whatever may be our desire. As fa r as the decision of winding up is 
concerned, it was to be decided in thre e compartments, one in the High Court, 
another in the Company Law Board and t he third one in the BIFR, as a last 
resort. But the important aspect of t he BIFR was that their major mandate was 
for the rehabilitation. I am not going in to the aspect of apportioning the blame 
but the fact remains that in a number of  cases which were registered with the 
BIFR, from 1987 to 2000, total number of cases were 3,068 and upto 1999, 
actual revival took place in 264 cases. About 375 cases were in the revival 
process and winding up was recommended in 741 cases. But the pending 
cases were almost more than one-third. It means that no decision was taken. It 
may be that they did not have the m andate, they did not have the teeth or 
whatever be the reason, but the fact remains that the decision could not be 
taken in most of the cases referred to these organisations, and as a result of 
which, large number, even here too, of  productive assets were either not 
utilised or in the process of being wasted. If I could understand it correctly - if I 
am wrong, the hon. Minister may correct  me - the Eradi Committee, an Expert 
Group, was suggested, separately, to prepare a special note in regard to the 
BIFR and as to what could be done. They considered that it would be desirable 
to combine all the three functions in one body so that there is  no multiplicity of 
the organisations and one does not work at cross purposes. In fact, we had - I 
am just telling about the Committee - an  opportunity of listening to a large 
section of the opinion-makers, opinion-builders and opinion-holders in the 
society. It is not that we only listened to the corporate sector. We devoted one 
full day - I hope my colleague, Shri Bhardwaj and other Members of the 
Committee would bear with me -for having an interaction with the trade union 
organisations. All the major Central trade union organisations responded to our 
invitation and they gave their suggestions. It is not that we had agreed to 
everybody's suggestion. We tried to find out how to resolve this problem and in 
what best manner these issues could be  resolved. That is why, we had 
recommended to the Government that this piece of legislation should be 
expedited. I am happy that with the consent of this House we would finally be 
able to pass this Bill. So far as the anom aly which is arising out of SICA is 
concerned, as the  hon.  Minist er has very correctly pointed out,  it  is  not that 
all the 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
provisions of this Amendment Bill wo uld be operationalised on the same day. 
So far as SICA is concerned, the rele vant provisions could be operationalised 
at the appropriate time. I am happy that such a provision has already been 
made in the Bill. I am glad that at the very beginning of the debate, the Finance 
Minister assured us about the continuat ion of employment of those who are 
working in the Company Law Board and other organisations. Of course, 
depending on their eligibility, they can go on deputation. Anyway, nobody is 
going to lose his job. The hon. Minister has already given this assurance. I 
would like to submit one thing for the c onsideration of the hon. Minister. Even 
after the Bill is passed, we shall have to consider very seriously as to how to 
re-address the sickness of industries and arrive at expeditious decisions. To 
my mind, what is important is, if we c an take decisions in time and prevent the 
sickness, the question of rehabilitation would be much easier. As you are 
doing major reforms in the banking sector and the financial sector, with the 
passage of the NPA Bill, the banks would be more accountable because they 
are the first organisation to understand the sickness of any industry from the 
irregular cash flow statement and other relevant documents. If steps could be 
initiated at that stage, perhaps, we woul d be able to resolve the problems at a 
lesser cost and we would be able to solve these problems in a very short time. 
This is one issue which we cannot ig nore because in our country we cannot 
provide social security and we cannot  create jobs as the developed countries 
can. That is why even in the uneconomic  sector, sometimes, continuation of 
employment and retention of employment  becomes necessary, as there is no 
other avenue open. Therefore, I s upport the Companies (Amendment) Bill 
which has been processed through the Parliamentary Standing Committee. 
So far as the second Bill in regard to producer companies is 
concerned, an apprehension was expressed whether through this exercise the 
cooperative movement was going to be a ffected, whether we were interfering 
with the cooperative character of t he organisations. The most important 
feature of this Bill is when we considered, because in our corporate culture, we 
have the concept of public sector companies, private limited companies, 
ownership, partnerships and a new concept of the producer companies having 
the flexibility of the cooperatives, were  thought of. And, many of the leading 
persons of cooperative movements, they wanted that existing cooperative laws 
are throttling the expansion and the deve lopment of the cooperative sector, 
especially the producer cooperative. 
256 

[17 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Therefore, an arrangement should be made, and it is optional; it is not 
mandatory. If somebody wants to conver t itself into a producer company, 
option lies with him, and it requires the special majority in the decisionmaking 
process and if they have that, in that pr ocess, if they go in for competition, and 
if they want to go in for competition, def initely they should have the flexibilities 
available to a company under the Companies Act. Because, cooperative laws 
are more restricting, the enormous powe rs which the registrar of cooperatives 
enjoy, and hardly any decision is being taken by the cooperatives themselves. 
And, within that rigid frame, despite the fact that a lot of concessions, in terms 
of money, in terms of liberty and flexib ility of functioning, were given, the 
movement has not attained the desired level. On the other hand, our corporate 
sector ought to face challenges from the different counterparts belonging to 
different countries with the opening up of  the economy. And, if our corporate 
laws are not in tune and they cannot provide adequate flexibility to the 
corporate sectors to be competitive, in cluding the producer companies in the 
cooperative sectors, then ultimately, we  won't be able to survive. Keeping 
these two basic objectives in view, and after a good deal of deliberations, we 
recommended these suggestions, and I am glad that most of the suggestions 
have been accepted by the Government. We understand that sometimes, all 
the suggestions cannot be accepted. Anybody will be quite happy if all the 
recommendations of the Standing Co mmittee are accommodated by the 
Government, but sometimes there are adm inistrative difficulties. But, by and 
large, the spirit of t he recommendations has been incorporated and with the 
passage of this law, I do feel that Indian corporate sector would be placed on a 
level playing field. They will have the opportunities of competing with the 
others and they will not be fettered by the legal framework which stand in the 
way, which stand in the way of the na tural growth and the development of the 
corporate sector, because India's industrialisation, our economic growth, much 
depend on how our corporate sector behav es; how they become competitive; 
how they become transparent; how they  become accountable; and, how the 
equity culture spreads all over the co untry. Almost 40 years ago, it was 
thought of and one organisation, which the other day, we had an opportunity of 
debating here. The whole purpose of UTI was to create equity culture in this 
country, to create awareness in this country. But because of bad management 
of the corporate sector, they failed to inspire confidence in the minds of the 
people, in the minds of the investors. And, many people invested their surplus 
money in dead assets like gold, but not in equity, 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2002] 
because they did not have confidence in the equity market. A series of 
measurements and enactments are necessary, and I must say, it cannot be 
'stop and go'. This is a constant exercise . With the changing world, with the 
changing environment within the country, outside the country, we should have 
the flexibility of adjusting our policies, changing our instrumentality to meet the 
requirements of the time. 
With these words, Mr. Chairman, Si r, I support both these Bills and I 
request the House to accept them. As  Chairman of the Standing Committee, I 
do feel, as their representative, I have this privilege of making this 
recommendation.   Thank you.
